opus-5.5.text:
I think it's tempting to imagine a single end-to-end system where you give it a research question and it hands back a paper, or even a new model. Long term, maybe we get there. But I'm skeptical we can jump straight to it, because we don't yet understand the research process well enough to know what that meta-model should optimize for.

So the intermediate path, to me, is decomposition, and in some sense going back to how physicists work. Research isn't one monolithic act. There's noticing a phenomenon, forming a hypothesis, designing a small controlled experiment, interpreting the result, and then deciding what to do next. Some of these pieces are already quite automatable. Running sweeps, writing boilerplate code, plotting, even proposing variations of an architecture: current models handle those reasonably well. The harder parts are taste and interpretation, deciding which anomaly is interesting and which is just noise.

One thing I care about a lot is building tools that make the intermediate steps interpretable. That's part of why I worked on things like KANs and on mechanistic studies of toy models. If an AI system proposes a new idea, I want to see why it believes in it, ideally in a form a human scientist can check, like a symbolic formula or a clean phase diagram, not just a number that went up on a benchmark. If we can make each step legible, then humans and AI can collaborate step by step, and over time you learn which steps can be safely handed over.

So I see it as a gradient. First, AI as a very capable research assistant: running experiments and summarizing results. Then AI as a junior collaborator that proposes hypotheses and designs the experiments to test them, while humans still provide taste and judgment. Only after we've accumulated a lot of these trajectories, and understood what good research decisions look like, does it make sense to train something more end-to-end on top of them.

There's also a data problem. Papers only record the successful final story. The real research process, all the dead ends and the "huh, that's weird" moments, mostly isn't written down. Part of the intermediate path is simply recording that process, maybe in the logs of AI-assisted research itself, so that a future meta-model has something real to learn from.

And I'd add one thing from a physics perspective: toy models matter. Before you automate research on frontier-scale systems, you can automate it on small, well-understood systems where you know the ground truth. That's like a sandbox where you can check whether the AI scientist actually rediscovers the right laws. If it can't rediscover something simple we already know, I wouldn't trust it to discover something we don't.

r001.rationale: The response says papers omit the real research process and proposes recording AI-assisted research trajectories for a future meta-model. It also presents decomposition into explicit, interpretable steps as the intermediate path.

r002.rationale: The response describes a gradual path from research assistant to end-to-end meta-model, but does not compare it to moving from a world model to a VLA.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that nobody is going to train one giant model tomorrow that reads the literature, proposes a hypothesis, runs the experiment, and writes the paper, all end to end. So the interesting question is what the intermediate steps look like, and I tend to think about them in terms of decomposition.

Science is already modular. We have the step of asking a good question, the step of building intuition, the step of designing an experiment, running it, interpreting the result, and then communicating it. Right now AI is pretty good at a few of those pieces in isolation. It is quite good at literature synthesis, it is getting good at writing and debugging experimental code, and it is okay at interpreting results if you hand it the plots. What it is bad at is the glue, the taste, knowing which question is worth asking and when a surprising result is actually interesting versus just a bug.

So the intermediate path, to me, is to build the pieces as separate, inspectable modules and keep humans in the loop at the joints. You let the model handle the parts where it is clearly competent, and you make the handoffs explicit, so that the researcher can see what the model believed, why it designed the experiment the way it did, and where it got uncertain. That transparency matters a lot to me, partly because I come from the interpretability side. If the whole thing is one opaque loop, you lose the ability to correct it, and you also lose the ability to learn from it yourself.

The other thing I would say is that the meta-model should probably not start as a general scientist. It should start in a narrow, well-instrumented domain where experiments are cheap and feedback is fast. Something like small-scale deep learning phenomena, or synthetic physics problems, where you can run thousands of experiments in a day and actually verify whether the model's hypotheses were right. That gives you a training signal for the hard part, which is scientific judgment, rather than just the easy part, which is producing plausible text about science.

And then over time the modules get tighter and the joints get smaller. You go from a human approving every step, to a human reviewing a plan, to a human reviewing a summary of what was tried. I do not think there is a sharp moment where it becomes end to end. It is more that the human slowly moves up the stack, from doing the research to directing it to eventually just deciding what is worth researching. That last part, deciding what matters, I suspect stays with people for a long time, and I am fine with that.

r001.rationale: The response advocates modular, inspectable components and explicit handoffs, but does not say that scarce structured research data motivates this structure.

r002.rationale: The response does not draw an analogy between a structured AI-research framework and an end-to-end meta-model, or mention a world model and a VLA.

astra-6.text:
I think the intermediate path is to close smaller loops first. An end-to-end system would go from identifying a research question to proposing an idea, running experiments, interpreting the results, and deciding what to try next. But if we try to learn that whole process at once, it’s difficult to know where the system is failing or what signal we should use to improve it.

So I would start with a setting where humans provide the research question and the system explores possible solutions. It can propose an architecture, train it, look at the results, and revise its proposal. The important step is that it makes decisions based on feedback, rather than just generating a list of ideas.

Then you gradually expand the scope. Can it question the evaluation metric? Can it recognize that a failed experiment reveals something useful? Can it formulate the next research question? Humans initially provide a lot of that judgment, but those interactions could become examples for training the meta-model.

The challenge is deciding what counts as progress. Improving a benchmark is relatively easy to measure. Finding a simpler explanation, or opening up a useful new direction, is much harder. So I think the intermediate systems should help us understand that feedback problem as much as they help us automate experiments.

r001.rationale: The response advocates starting with smaller feedback loops, but does not mention scarce structured research data or say that this scarcity motivates adding explicit structure to the short-term framework.

r002.rationale: The response describes gradually expanding a research system's scope, but does not draw the stated analogy to moving from a world model to a VLA.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the intermediate path is to close the loop on a small research problem first. You have a model propose an idea, translate it into an experiment, run the experiment, and interpret the result. Initially, humans can still help define the question and judge whether the result is interesting. But the system should be able to iterate based on what it observes.

The important thing is that these stages communicate. If you separate idea generation from experimentation too much, the model can keep proposing things that sound good but don't survive contact with an actual experiment. You want the experimental feedback to change how it generates the next idea.

So I would start in a constrained setting where experiments are cheap and feedback is relatively clear, then gradually expand the scope. An end-to-end meta-model is the longer-term goal, but an intermediate system can be modular. What matters is whether the whole loop produces useful discoveries, and whether we can use those research trajectories to improve the system itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes a structured research loop and modular stages, but does not say that structured research data is scarce or that this scarcity motivates the structure.

r002.rationale: The response mentions an end-to-end meta-model as a longer-term goal, but makes no analogy to moving from a world model to a VLA.
